summary: Updates RFC 2131 to fix an issue with its rule that a DHCP server must not return the client identifier option to the client. The document addresses problems that rule caused, allowing servers to echo the option in replies.

eli5.summary: When you give your name at a desk, the clerk was told never to say it back. This fixes that rule so the clerk may repeat it to confirm.

questions: should a dhcp server return the client identifier option
what changed in rfc 2131 about client identifier
why is chaddr zero in dhcp

subtitle: DHCP servers must now echo the client identifier option back to clients that sent it.

tldr.problem: RFC 2131 said servers MUST NOT return the client identifier option, which left relay agents and clients unable to tell whom a reply was for when the hardware address field was all zeroes.
tldr.mechanism: If a client sent a client identifier, the server MUST return it unaltered in its reply, and the client MUST silently discard a reply whose identifier does not match its own.
tldr.outcome: RFC 2131 is updated so replies can be matched to the right client, with a small, accepted risk that some client might drop the formerly unexpected option.

facts.label: Server rule
facts.value: Echo the client identifier unaltered if the client sent one

facts.label: Client rule
facts.value: Silently discard replies with a mismatched identifier

today: RFC 6842 is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 2131. The metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: The Problem with Replies
sections.content:
In RFC 2131, a combination of the client identifier option or chaddr and the assigned network address identifies a client's lease. The same RFC says a server MUST NOT return the client identifier option in DHCPOFFER and DHCPACK messages, and that relay agents and servers MAY drop packets that have neither client identifier nor chaddr.

Some clients, such as a mobile phone or tablet, have no valid hardware address and set chaddr to all zeroes. They set the client identifier instead. Replies without it may be dropped at a relay agent, and the client cannot be sure a reply is meant for it, because xid values from different clients in a subnet need not be unique. Multiple DHCP clients sharing one host and one chaddr are affected too.
sections.eli5: Some devices have no proper name tag, so they write a nickname instead. If replies leave the nickname off, nobody can tell who the reply is for.

sections.title: The Modification to RFC 2131
sections.content:
If the client identifier option is present in a message from a client, the server MUST return it, unaltered, in its response. If the client did not send it, the server still MUST NOT include it. This applies to DHCPOFFER, DHCPACK and DHCPNAK, and the RFC revises the table from Section 4.3.1 of RFC 2131 accordingly.

On the client side, when a DHCP message contains a client identifier option, the client MUST compare it to the one it is configured to send. If they do not match, the client MUST silently discard the message.
sections.eli5: If you gave a nickname, the clerk must say it back exactly. If you hear a different nickname, you ignore that answer.

sections.title: Why the Old Rule Existed
sections.content:
The RFC explains that the old requirement was made purely to conserve the limited space in the packet. The new behavior is in line with DHCPv6 (RFC 3315), where the server always includes the Client Identifier option in Reply messages.

It admits that clients might drop packets containing the formerly unexpected option, though this is unlikely. No known client implementations do so, and the authors judge that more harm comes from leaving the option out than from adding it.
sections.eli5: The old rule was just to save a little room in the envelope. The authors decided the room is worth spending.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The document adds no new security considerations beyond those in RFC 2131. It notes that clients connect to many networks without knowing which, so the client identifier is routinely shared with network operators and could be used in ways that violate the user's privacy. That problem existed in RFC 2131, and this document does nothing to address it.
sections.eli5: Telling every network your nickname can be a privacy problem. This RFC does not fix that.
